body.hook: In 1912, Pablo Picasso glued a piece of printed oilcloth into a painting, and collage entered fine art. Since then, artists have combined paint, paper, photographs, fabric, found objects and even digital prints. Mixed media lets you mix materials to say more than one medium alone.

study.title: Layer It Up
study.question: How does combining media change what an artwork can say?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Look: Hannah Höch's photomontages (Germany, about 1919) cut and rearrange magazine photos to comment on society; Romare Bearden's collages (United States, 1960s) combine painted paper and photographs to show community life.
2. Media sampler (20 minutes): On a page divided into six boxes, test combinations: watercolour + oil pastel resist; tissue paper + glue layers; magazine collage + pencil drawing; acrylic + texture paste or sand; ink + found paper (maps, music sheets, newspapers); and a photocopy transfer.
3. Small work (30 minutes): Create a 15 cm × 20 cm artwork on a theme (my neighbourhood, technology, nature, memory) combining at least three media. Plan layers from background to foreground.

body.objective: Students will be able to use emphasis and unity.
body.iCan: I can use emphasis and unity.
successCriteria: I can create a clear focal point in a mixed-media work
I can use colour, repetition and theme to create unity

body.hook: Mixed media can easily turn into a messy pile of stuff. What makes some collages powerful and others chaotic? Two principles: emphasis, which gives the eye a place to land, and unity, which makes everything feel like one artwork.

vocabulary.definition: Making one area stand out as the focal point.
The sense that all parts of an artwork belong together.
The area the eye goes to first.
A planned set of colours, such as analogous or complementary.

The order in which the eye sees parts of an artwork.

study.title: Focus and Belonging
study.question: How do emphasis and unity make mixed media work?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Compare (10 minutes): Look at two collages: one chaotic (many colours, no clear focus) and one unified (limited colours, one focal point, repeated shapes). List what makes the difference.
2. Emphasis toolkit: create a focal point using contrast (light against dark), isolation (one item alone in space), placement (near the centre or at a rule-of-thirds point), size, or detail.
3. Unity toolkit: a limited colour scheme (analogous or complementary), repeated shapes or textures, a consistent theme, overlapping pieces, and a unifying wash of colour over everything.
4. Revise (35 minutes): Take your mixed-media work from last lesson, photograph it, then improve it: strengthen one focal point and add two unity techniques. Photograph it again to compare.

body.objective: Students will be able to develop a series of related works.
body.iCan: I can develop a series of related works.
successCriteria: I can explain why artists work in series
I can plan a series of three related works

body.hook: Claude Monet painted the same haystacks over and over in 1890–1891, at sunrise, in snow, in fog, at sunset. One painting is a picture; a series is an investigation. Artists use series to explore an idea from many angles.

vocabulary.definition: A group of related artworks that explore one idea.
The central idea that connects a series.
Changes from one work to the next.

Exploring an idea in depth by trying different approaches.

study.title: Three Ways of Seeing
study.question: How can a series explore one idea in depth?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Look: Claude Monet's Haystacks series (1890–1891); Andy Warhol's repeated soup cans (1962); Lawren Harris's paintings of Lake Superior. Discuss what stays the same and what changes.
2. Choose a theme: an object, a place, a person, a feeling or an issue (for example, my street at three times of day; a shoe as old, new and imagined; climate in three seasons).
3. Decide consistency and variation: Keep 2–3 things the same (size, medium, subject or composition) and change 1–2 things (colour scheme, time of day, viewpoint, mood, style).
4. Thumbnails (15 minutes): Plan all three works on one page.
5. Create (two lessons): Make three works about 15 cm × 20 cm, mixed media allowed. Display them side by side as a triptych.
